report:
**Conclusion:** The answer is **yes, probably**—when mask wearing is substantially increased across a community, evidence indicates it can reduce SARS‑CoV‑2 infections. The effect is not absolute and depends on mask type, fit, consistent use, ventilation, crowding, and whether people are actually wearing them.

The strongest direct evidence is a large cluster-randomized trial in rural Bangladesh (600 villages; 342,126 adults). A community program that distributed and promoted masks increased observed masking and reduced *symptomatic, antibody-confirmed* COVID-19. The reduction was clearer for surgical masks and among older adults. Because it randomized villages rather than merely comparing people who chose to mask, it provides relatively strong causal evidence for a population-level effect.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9036942/

A systematic review of community evidence likewise concluded that ecological studies supported a protective effect and that mask policies *may* lower SARS‑CoV‑2 burden at population level, though much of that evidence was observational and therefore susceptible to confounding (e.g., other precautions changing at the same time).  
https://www.thelancet.com/pdfs/journals/eclinm/PIIS2589-5370(21)00304-7.pdf

Why some say “no”: the 2023 Cochrane review found randomized evidence across respiratory viruses did not show a clear average benefit for masks versus no masks. But that is not proof of no effect: its trials span different viruses and settings, and adherence, mask quality, timing, and concurrent interventions varied substantially. Its conclusions should not override the large SARS‑CoV‑2-specific Bangladesh trial.  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD006207.pub6/full

So, “masks cannot reduce infections when widely worn” is not supported. A more accurate claim is that they are one imperfect layer of protection, with the best evidence favoring a modest population benefit when uptake is high.
